agent.reply: Understood. I'll add a field so you can record the actual amount received when marking an invoice as paid, rather than only matching the exact invoice amount. This will help your app accurately reflect what you received and make reconciliation with your bank statement easier.
plan: Update the database to allow payment records linked to invoices to store both 'invoice amount' and 'amount received'.
On the payment-entry screen, add an 'Amount Received' field, defaulting to the invoice amount but editable.
Show the total amount received on the invoice details page, and if it's greater than the invoice, flag it as an overpayment/rounding.
Update reports to show total received and allow reconciliation to your bank statement.
Test with a few edge cases: e.g., amount received is greater, equal to, or (rarely) less than the invoice amount.

agent.reply: Great idea! Giving your clients access to make minor corrections themselves will save everyone time and improve their experience. Here’s how we’ll approach this change:
plan: Add a client login: Create secure accounts for clients so they can log in, likely using their email addresses.
Permission control: Limit client edits to only their own invoices and data.
Editable fields: Allow clients to edit specific information (contact name, service description) but protect financial values like amounts due, dates, etc.
Update data model: Track who made each change with timestamps, so you have an audit trail for compliance/review.
Build a client portal screen: Simple, clear interface where clients can view and edit their allowed details, possibly requiring confirmation before saving changes.
Notifications: Optionally send you (the owner) a summary of changes made by clients for your records.
Edge cases: Add checks so clients cannot make changes if an invoice has already been paid or officially submitted to tax authorities.

agent.reply: We'll add a 'Quick Close' button for each invoice, letting you mark it as Paid with one click, right from the invoice list. I'll make sure this action is fast so the dashboard stays tidy, but you can still add payment details later if needed. The steps below explain how we'll do this.
plan: 1. Add a 'Quick Close' button to each row in the invoice list UI.
2. When clicked, immediately set the invoice status to 'Paid'.
3. Store a flag (e.g., 'quick_closed': true) so we know which invoices were quick closed without payment details.
4. Make sure 'quick closed' invoices remain editable to allow adding payment details later.
5. Update the dashboard so these invoices no longer show as open/unpaid.
6. Consider edge cases: e.g., block the button if the invoice is already marked Paid, and confirm quick close works for bulk actions if needed.
7. Test for usability to confirm it's fast and doesn't introduce confusion.

agent.reply: Great, I’ll add the ability to create flat-fee invoices for those clients. This will allow you to enter just the amount and a description—no itemized details. Flat-fee invoices will be clearly labeled and simple to send and track.
plan: Add a 'Flat Fee Invoice' option to the 'Create Invoice' page alongside the current detailed invoice option.
Update the invoice data model to support a new type indicator (e.g., 'flat_fee' vs. 'itemized') and allow invoices with only amount and description when 'flat_fee' is selected.
In the UI, simplify the form when 'Flat Fee' is chosen: show fields for amount and client, and a single description box; hide line items.
Ensure PDF/print/email output for flat-fee invoices just shows the description and total, no breakdown or itemized sections.
Add validation/test cases ensuring flat-fee invoices can be created and paid, but are clearly distinguished from itemized ones both internally and for clients.

agent.reply:
Understood: You want recurring retainer invoices to be generated and sent automatically for your twelve clients on the 1st of each month. This will save you time by eliminating manual data entry.

To address this, I'll add a recurring invoice feature that allows you to schedule repeat invoices for specific clients with predefined details.
plan: Add a 'Recurring Invoice' option to the invoice creation screen, where you can set frequency (e.g., monthly), clients, line items, and send date.
Extend the data model with new tables (e.g., RecurringInvoiceTemplate) to store recurring invoice details (client, template, next send date, etc.).
Implement a scheduled backend process that runs on the 1st of each month: looks up active recurring invoice templates, creates invoices, and triggers sending emails to clients.
Add management UI to view/edit/cancel recurring templates (in case you need to update the details or stop the recurrence).
Handle edge cases: paused clients, changed rates, templates with missing data, and send failure notifications.
Deploy and test thoroughly with one template before setting up all twelve.

agent.reply: Great idea—adding a 'Pay Now' button with card payment will make things much easier for your clients. Here’s how I’ll tackle it:
plan: Select and integrate a payment processor (like Stripe or Square) to handle secure card payments.
Update the invoice data model to track payment status, transaction ID, and payment method.
Add a 'Pay Now' button to the invoice screen (both web and mobile if applicable).
Design a secure payment form that appears when clients click 'Pay Now'.
Handle payment confirmations, errors, and update invoice status accordingly.
Send confirmation emails/receipts to clients after a successful payment.
Test edge cases: duplicate payments, failed transactions, invoice already paid, expired invoices.
Ensure Payment Card Industry (PCI) compliance (handled by payment processor).

agent.reply: Great idea! Adding a filter for overdue and unpaid invoices will make it much easier to track outstanding payments. To do this, I’d update the invoice list UI, adjust how we fetch invoice data, and make sure the filter logic handles edge cases (like due today or invoices partially paid).
plan: Add a filter control (e.g., a checkbox or dropdown option) to the invoice list screen labeled 'Show overdue & unpaid only'.
Update the backend query (or API call) so that when this filter is active, only invoices where 'due date' < today AND 'status' is unpaid are returned.
Confirm our data model tracks invoice status and due date, and address cases like partial payments (if applicable, ensure only invoices with an unpaid balance are shown).
Test for edge cases: invoices due today, invoices paid moments ago, time zone differences.
Update frontend to show when this filter is applied (e.g., a banner or tag), and confirm the count matches expectations.
Deploy and let you review the feature in staging before going live.

agent.reply:
Absolutely, we can support this. We'll add a way for you to record a bank transfer payment against an invoice, including the payment date and amount. This ensures your records are accurate and can handle payments that may not exactly match the invoice (e.g., partial payments or overpayments).

Here's how we'll approach this:
plan: Add a 'Record Payment' button or link on each invoice page.
Create a simple payment entry form that lets you select: 1) the payment method (e.g., bank transfer), 2) the date the payment landed, and 3) the amount received.
Update the data model to store payments as a related table (e.g., Payment: id, invoice_id, amount, payment_date, payment_method).
On each invoice screen, display the payment(s) recorded, total paid, and any outstanding balance.
Handle edge cases: allow for partial payments, flag overpayments, and make sure invoices update to 'Paid' only when fully paid.

agent.reply: I will add a way to record the actual amount received against each invoice, separate from the invoice's total. This ensures your records match your bank statement, even when clients pay more (or less) than the invoice total. Here's how we'll handle it:
plan: 1. Update the Invoice data model to add an optional 'amount_received' field (decimal), which records the exact payment received from the client.
2. Update invoice screens: When marking an invoice as 'Paid,' prompt the user to enter the actual amount received. Default to the invoice total but allow editing.
3. Display the recorded amount received (and any difference from the invoice total, flagged as 'overpayment' or 'underpayment') on the invoice detail and report views.
4. Update reporting to use 'amount_received' for payment totals and to flag/track over and underpayments for reconciliation.

5. Handle edge cases: If amount received < invoice total, invoice stays marked as Paid (as per current process), but highlight the shortfall. If > invoice total, show the excess as an overpayment in reports.
6. Ensure exported data and audit trails reflect both the invoice amount and amount received for accurate record-keeping.

agent.reply: To address this request, I propose adding a limited-access self-service portal for clients, allowing them to update their contact details and request corrections for invoice service descriptions (not direct editing for legal/audit reasons). This ensures control and auditability while reducing your admin workload. Here’s how this change would be implemented:
plan: 1. Add a new entity: 'Client Portal User' with email/password authentication (invite sent to client).
2. Modify client record: add fields for portal enablement and invite status.
3. Implement portal screens: a) View and edit own contact info; b) View invoices and submit correction requests for line items (not direct edits, but suggestions sent to you for approval/merge).
4. Notification system: notify bookkeeper when a correction is suggested; allow quick review and approval in the app.
5. Update audit logs: capture all edits and requests for compliance.
6. Edge cases: Only client email/contact details editable by client; invoice line items can be suggested for change but not altered directly. Bookkeeper can deny/accept suggestions.
7. Update data model and API to support correction requests and client contact edits with appropriate permissions.

agent.reply:
Understood. I’ll add a ‘Quick close’ button to the invoice list screen so you can mark invoices as Paid with a single click, making month-end closing more efficient.

Here’s how I’ll approach this:

1. Add a ‘Quick close’ button/action beside each invoice in the main invoice list (where actions like View or Edit are).
2. When clicked, the system will immediately update the invoice status to Paid, without opening the invoice detail screen or requiring additional input.
3. To prevent mistakes, I’ll include a brief confirmation (e.g., a popup that says: “Mark invoice #123 as Paid?” Yes/Cancel).
4. ‘Quick close’ will only be enabled for invoices currently in the Sent or Overdue status (never for Draft or already Paid invoices, since status changes are single-directional per requirements).
5. The invoice list will refresh to reflect the status change instantly and remove/apply any visual badges as appropriate.
6. All existing data (like payment notes or method) can be filled in/edited later, if needed—status update doesn’t lock the record from further detail entry.

No change to the underlying data model is required (just an update to the existing status field). I’ll ensure this works with audit logs so you can always see who marked it as Paid and when.
plan: Add ‘Quick close’ button/action to each non-final invoice in the list view.
On click, prompt user with a confirmation dialog (‘Mark as Paid?’).
If confirmed, update the invoice status from Sent/Overdue to Paid.
Refresh the invoice list to reflect new status immediately.
Disallow ‘Quick close’ on Draft or Paid invoices.
Audit the action for tracking who performed it and when.

judge.citation: status changes are single-directional per requirements

agent.reply:
We'll add support for flat-fee invoices, allowing you to enter just a description and total amount (without itemizing quantity, unit price, or tax). The system will ensure these meet your workflow but still align with required invoice fields.

Here's how we’ll proceed:
plan: Update the invoice creation UI to offer a 'Flat Fee' option alongside standard itemized invoices.
For flat-fee invoices, show fields for 'Description' and 'Amount Only'. Tax rate may be optional or omitted if not needed (to confirm).
Adjust the Invoice Line Item data model to allow line items with amount/description only (with quantity/unit price/tax rate set null or defaulted) when flat-fee is selected.
Ensure invoices can consist of a single flat-fee line item and still comply with 'at least one line item' requirement.
Clearly distinguish flat-fee invoices in preview, PDF, and client-facing emails (show only the description and total).
Review reporting and filters to include both invoice types, ensuring amounts and statuses calculate correctly.
Test for edge cases: mixing flat-fee with itemized lines (likely disallow, to keep it simple), validation, and required fields.

agent.reply:
I propose to add a recurring invoices feature so retainer invoices for the twelve clients are automatically generated and emailed on the 1st of each month. This will save time and prevent manual re-keying every month.

Here’s how we’ll deliver this:
- Add a “Recurring Invoice” screen where you can set up template invoices for each client (line items, amounts, etc.) and specify schedule details (e.g., monthly on the 1st, start date, optional end date).
- Store recurring invoice templates in a new data model (with references to clients and all invoice fields except the unique invoice number and actual issue/due dates).
- On the 1st of each month, the system will generate invoices based on each template (assigning a unique invoice number, correct issue/due date, line items, client, etc.), set status to "Sent," and email them to each client.
- Allow editing or disabling recurring templates at any time.
- Log auto-generated invoice activity for audit trail.
- Show generated recurring invoices in the regular invoices list, clearly linked to their template.

Edge cases: Clients added/removed from recurring list, template changes mid-cycle, handling email bounces.
plan: Add a new Recurring Invoice Template data model (client ref, line items, schedule)
Create UI to let users configure/edit recurring templates
Implement monthly scheduler to trigger invoice generation and sending
Generate and send invoices automatically (assign invoice number/issue/due dates)
Ensure recurring invoices appear in the invoices list and are tracked like manual ones
Allow viewing, editing, and disabling recurring templates
Handle edge cases—client removal, template updates, and notification of failed deliveries

agent.reply: Thanks for the suggestion. Currently, our app doesn't handle payment processing (per the project scope), so clients can't pay invoices by card directly in the app. Supporting this request involves integrating a payment provider (like Stripe or PayPal) and handling payment flows. If you decide to include this feature, here's what it would involve:
plan: Update the scope and get approval to add payment processing (if you want to proceed).
Research and choose a payment provider (e.g., Stripe, PayPal) suitable for small businesses and your firm's needs.
Register for a developer account and set up the necessary payment API credentials.
Update the invoice template to include a 'Pay Now' button with a secure payment link (preferably unique per invoice).
Modify the backend to generate payment sessions for each invoice and track payments upon completion.
Update the data model to record payment transaction details on the invoice (e.g., payment date, transaction ID, amount).
Handle confirmation callbacks from the payment provider to automatically mark invoices as 'Paid' in the system once card payment is confirmed.
Review privacy/data handling changes for compliance.
Test the full flow end-to-end with sample invoices and card payments.

judge.conflict_description: The engineer states the app doesn't handle payment processing per the project scope, so card payments aren't currently supported.

agent.reply:
I understand—you want to quickly see invoices that are overdue and still awaiting payment. I will add a filter option to the invoice list screen to display exactly that: all invoices where the due date has passed and status is not Paid.

Here’s what I will do:
plan: Update the invoice query logic on the back end to allow filtering for invoices where due date < today and status is not Paid (i.e., show Overdue, and any Sent invoices past due date).
Update the UI for the invoice list to add a filter checkbox or dropdown option: 'Show overdue & unpaid invoices only'.
If selected, the invoice list should show only matching invoices; if no matches, display a message like 'No overdue unpaid invoices at this time.'
Edge Case: Ensure newly sent invoices are not included unless their due date has passed and they are not Paid.
Test the filter with sample data to confirm it works for all relevant statuses (Sent, Overdue) and does not include Paid invoices.
Document the filter in the help/tour so users know how to access it.

agent.reply:
We'll add the ability to record payment details (date received, amount, and associated invoice) when you mark an invoice as paid. This will keep payment records organized and auditable, meeting your need to track real-world payments that arrive by bank transfer.

The data model does not currently have an explicit 'Payment' entity, so we'll add that. The UI for marking an invoice as "Paid" will update to prompt for the required information.
plan: 1. Add a Payment entity: Fields: payment_date (required), amount (required), invoice_id (required; reference to Invoice).
2. Update Invoice screen: When marking an invoice as Paid, show a dialog to collect payment date and amount before confirming status change.
3. Validate inputs: Ensure the amount cannot exceed the invoice total (potential overpayments can be handled in a future release if needed).
4. Save Payment record and tie it to the invoice; update the invoice status as Paid.
5. Update reports/analytics to show payment details as needed.

agent.reply: Thanks for raising this—tracking the real amount received is an important feature for reconciling with bank statements. I'll add a 'Received Amount' field to each invoice, so you can record what the client actually paid, even if it's different from the billed amount.
plan: Update the Invoice data model: Add a 'received_amount' (decimal/currency) field, defaulting to NULL or 0.

Modify the UI on the invoice details/edit screen: Add an input field for 'Amount Received'. Display this field for existing invoices (not required when creating a new invoice, but can be edited after payment arrives).
Update the invoice list screen: Optionally show a column for 'Amount Received' to highlight paid/overpaid invoices.
Add validation: Ensure 'Amount Received' cannot be negative, and flag if it's less than or more than the invoice amount.
Test edge cases: Entering 0, exact invoice amount, or excess (round-up), and verify display and calculations.
Update documentation and help text so users know how and when to enter 'Amount Received'.

agent.reply: Based on your request, this involves introducing client accounts so clients can log in and edit their invoice details. This change significantly expands the scope and alters several core decisions—currently, only firm staff can access invoices, and there are no external client accounts. Allowing clients to log in and edit invoice data directly would require new user roles, security considerations, and workflow changes. If you'd like to move forward, I’ll outline what needs to change to support this scenario.
plan: Update requirements to support external client accounts and user roles (client vs. firm staff).
Extend the authentication system for external clients, including registration and password management.
Modify invoice access controls so clients can only access and edit their own invoices (and only fields relevant to them, such as contact name and service descriptions).
Design new UI screens for client login and editing invoice details.
Add audit tracking: log who made changes to invoices (firm staff or client).
Modify testing and validation procedures to cover client interactions, permissions, and error cases.
Revisit documentation and onboarding for clients.
Communicate to existing firm staff about the upcoming changes and get feedback on security and workflow.

judge.conflict_description: The request contradicts the existing decision that only firm staff can access invoices and that there are no external client accounts.

agent.reply: Understood. I’ll add a 'Quick close' button to the invoice list so you can mark invoices as Paid with one click, helping you quickly clear settled ones at month end. The paid status will be visible in the list, and invoice details can be updated later if needed.
plan: Update the invoice data model to include a 'status' field (e.g., Unpaid/Paid).
Add a 'Quick close' button next to each invoice in the invoice list UI.
When clicked, 'Quick close' sets invoice status to Paid (without requiring entry of payment details).
Update the invoice list to visually indicate which invoices are marked as Paid.
Allow editing of invoices after marking as Paid, in case you want to add payment details later.
Add automated tests for the new status and update process.
Manual walkthrough: confirm button works, status updates, and invoices can be edited after quick close.
Update documentation to explain the Quick close workflow.

agent.reply:
We'll add support for flat-fee invoices so you can quickly bill retainer clients without itemizing services. The change will allow you to select 'flat-fee' when creating an invoice and enter a single amount and description, skipping the itemized service list. These invoices will look professional and stay aligned with your firm's branding and tone.

Here's how we'll approach this:
plan: Update the invoice data model to allow 'flat-fee' or 'itemized' invoice types, storing amount and description for flat-fee invoices.
Modify the invoice creation and editing screens to include a toggle/option for 'flat-fee' or 'itemized' invoice; show only relevant fields (amount, description) for flat-fee.
Adjust invoice viewing and template rendering to display flat-fee invoices with the amount and description, omitting itemized service lists.
Update validation to ensure required fields are present for flat-fee invoices (amount, description, client, due date).
Test edge cases, e.g. switching invoice types, incomplete information, branding application, and ensure clear/professional messaging throughout.
Update documentation to include the new flat-fee workflow.

agent.reply: We'll add a recurring invoice feature for automatic generation and sending to your regular clients. This will reduce manual work and ensure timely delivery each month. Here’s how we’ll handle it:
plan: 1. Update data model: Add a 'recurring invoice' option, recurrence interval (e.g., monthly), and scheduling details to the invoice schema. Link each recurring invoice to its client and service items.

2. UI changes: Add a form to create/edit a recurring invoice, specifying client, services, and frequency (monthly, 1st of month). Clearly indicate which invoices are recurring in the invoice list and settings.
3. Automation logic: Build a background job or scheduled task that, on the 1st of each month, generates new invoices based on the recurring templates and marks them as generated for tracking.
4. Sending logic: Trigger email delivery for each generated invoice to assigned clients (using existing mail infrastructure). Log success/failure and notify staff if any issue occurs.
5. Edge cases: Validate that recurring invoices handle holidays/weekends (if any rules apply), skipped months, and duplicate prevention. Let users edit, pause, or stop recurring schedules.
6. Testing: Unit and integration tests for auto-generation and sending; manual walkthrough on the 1st simulating client delivery.
7. Documentation: Update user guide with steps to set up/manage recurring invoices.

2. Update invoice creation and editing screens so firm staff can set or update the payment status for each invoice.

agent.reply: To support entering client payments, I will add a payment tracking feature. This will let firm staff record payments received by bank transfer, linking each payment to the relevant invoice. We'll display payments on the invoice view so staff can see payment history and outstanding amount. The app won't handle payment processing, just internal recording for bookkeeping clarity.
plan: Extend the data model: Add a Payment record with fields: payment date, amount, invoice reference, and payment type (bank transfer).
Update UI: Add 'Record Payment' option on each invoice. Build a modal/form to input payment date and amount.
Update invoice view: Show linked payments as a list under each invoice, showing payment date, amount, and payment method. Show outstanding amount (total minus payments).
Validation: Ensure payments cannot exceed invoice total; handle cases of partial payment and full payment.
Testing: Add tests for payment recording, linking, and validation; manual walkthrough for edge cases (overpayment, multiple payments, missing info).
Update documentation: Describe payment entry and display features.

agent.reply:
To accommodate client 'rounding up', we'll let Bookkeepers and Owners record a payment amount that exceeds the invoice's Amount Due, while maintaining strict accounting: the invoice is still marked 'Paid' when the full amount due is received; any 'extra' received will be tracked and visible but not treated as payment for future invoices. 

We’ll:
- Update the Payment form to allow entry of an amount that can exceed invoice amount, but add a new field for 'excess' (e.g. tip/gift).
- Adjust validation to permit overpayment, but mark the 'excess' amount separately.
- Show both 'Amount Due', 'Amount Received', and 'Excess' on the Payment record and, optionally, on the Invoice view.
- Prevent use of excess payments for subsequent invoices (no credits/refunds).
- Preserve audit trail and reporting for actual funds received and invoiced amounts.

Edge cases handled: partial payments (still not supported), overpayments only tracked—not applied/funded elsewhere.

This change will mean your books reflect what really came in, with clear separation between invoiced and received amounts.
plan: Add a new optional 'Excess Received' field to the Payment entity (data model).
Update Payment creation/edit form to allow entry of an amount > invoice 'Amount Due', and auto-calculate/display 'Excess Received'.
Revise Invoice status logic: Invoice becomes 'Paid' when payment >= amount due, but only the original amount due is counted as 'settled'.
Update the Invoice and Payment views to show 'Amount Due', 'Amount Received', and 'Excess'.
Update reporting/dashboard logic to distinguish between invoiced and received totals (and, optionally, excess/tips).
Document this new flow for your team and clients, so all users understand what 'excess' means.

agent.reply:
As requested, you want clients to be able to edit their own contact information and service entry descriptions. However, per the current design, clients are only allowed to view/pay invoices and see service entries—they cannot edit any records (see rules r1, g2, client_portal_scope). Allowing clients to edit would require a shift in role permissions and data integrity rules. Here is what I'd propose and the exact steps needed if you'd like to move forward:

I will:
1. Update the Design Sheet and Spec to permit client editing for their contact information (Client Record) and service entry descriptions (attached to their own invoices).
2. Add role permissions so clients can edit their own Client Record and Service Entry descriptions (but only ones linked to their invoices).
3. Update the API and UI to enable these edits, limiting them to just those fields and their own records.
4. Add audit logging to record client edits for traceability.
5. Review edge cases: prevent clients from editing anything once an invoice is marked 'Paid', and block edits to records not belonging to them, ensuring compliance with data integrity.

If you'd like to proceed, I'll first revise the design docs, then plan with engineering to roll out these permissions safely.
plan: Update Design Sheet/spec to permit client editing of their own contact info and service entry descriptions.
Add role permissions so clients can edit only their own records, and only non-financial fields.
Update UI/API to allow these client edits (Client Record: contact name/email/phone/address; Service Entry: description).
Audit log all client edits for traceability.
Disallow edits on records attached to 'Paid' invoices to maintain invoice integrity.
Review for compliance with linked rules; update acceptance tests for new client actions.

judge.conflict_description: The request to let clients edit their contact info and service descriptions conflicts with the current design where clients are only allowed to view/pay invoices and cannot edit any records.

agent.reply:
We can add a 'Quick close' button to the invoice list so you can mark an invoice as Paid in one click, making your month-end process more efficient. However, our current rules require that an invoice can only be marked as 'Paid' after a payment is recorded (and only payments equal to the exact invoice amount are allowed). Allowing a one-click 'Paid' action without a payment record would break an integrity rule and core audit logic (see R-5 in the spec).

To address your need and maintain system integrity, here's a practical path: the 'Quick close' button will open a small dialog pre-filled with the invoice details (amount, due date, method defaulted to 'Quick Close' or configurable), so you only have to review and click 'Confirm'. This both creates the required Payment record and marks the invoice as Paid, all in one streamlined step. This way, all system invariants and audit requirements are respected, but you get a much faster workflow for clearing out settled invoices.
plan: Add a 'Quick close' button directly to each row in the invoice list (visible to Firm Owner/Bookkeeper when status is 'Sent').
On click, display a minimal dialog showing invoice amount (pre-filled, read-only), payment date (defaults to today), method (defaults to 'Quick Close', editable), and confirm/cancel.
On confirm, automatically create a Payment record for that invoice (amount = invoice amount_due, method = entered or default), complying with business rules.
Update the invoice status to 'Paid' after the payment is recorded (as per R-5).
Refresh the invoice list to remove/grey out invoices that are now marked as Paid.
Edge cases: Block 'Quick close' for invoices already marked as 'Paid', show error if any invariant would be violated, ensure changes are tracked in audit fields (who/when).

judge.conflict_description: A one-click 'Paid' action without a payment record would violate the integrity rule that an invoice can only be marked Paid after a payment equal to the exact invoice amount is recorded.

agent.reply:
I understand the need for flat-fee invoices without a breakdown. To enable this (while preserving system data integrity), I’ll add support for a special "flat fee" Service Entry type that allows invoices to have a single description and amount—no hours/rate breakdown. This keeps compatibility with rules (every invoice needs at least one Service Entry; clients still don’t edit entries).

Here’s what I’ll do:

1. Add a UI option when creating a Service Entry: “Flat fee” vs. “Hourly.” Selecting 'Flat fee' disables hours and rate, enabling just amount and description.
2. Update the Service Entry data model to support an optional flat_fee_amount field (with validation so either hours/rate or flat_fee_amount is required, not both).
3. Change the Invoice creation flow: Bookkeeper can add a single “Flat fee” Service Entry instead of the standard ones. Invoice summary shows only the description and flat fee total.
4. On client-facing PDFs/portal: If the invoice is only a flat-fee entry, hide the breakdown and just show the description and total.

Edge cases:
- Editing: Flat-fee Service Entries are editable until the invoice is Paid, like others.
- Existing rules (e.g., invoice must cite a Service Entry) are preserved.
- Flat-fee and hourly Service Entries can’t mix on the same invoice—UI prevents it for simplicity, unless you want mixing allowed.
